The platform at Nagpur station was packed, and the train was pulling in with a long, loud horn. Five-year-old Yamini was hopping about, pointing at a balloon seller.
Chetan's first thought was to shout a long list: stay close, don't run, the train is coming, hold the bag. Instead he crouched down until his face was level with hers, put a hand on her shoulder, and said calmly, "Yamini. Hold my hand."
Then he waited.
Yamini looked at him, then at the train, and slid her small hand into his.
"Good," he said. They stepped on together.

qa.a: Yamini was pointing at a balloon seller.

qa.q: Why might Yamini have taken Chetan's hand at once?
qa.a: She likely felt calm and safe because he came down to her eye level and spoke one clear instruction instead of shouting.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Crouching, giving one short instruction and waiting worked better than a long list, which Yamini could not have followed in the noise.

qa.q: What would change if Chetan had shouted a list from above?
qa.a: Yamini might have felt confused or scared by the noise and the words, and might not have listened in time.

grounding: An adult crouches to a child's eye level, gives one short calm instruction and waits, and the child listens.

In the village, the doctor's jeep had come twice in one week, and nine-year-old Chaitanya had started lying awake. He heard whispers at night: "hospital," "the town," "we'll see." In the morning everyone smiled too much.
One evening, his mother, Rashmi, found him sitting on the cattle-shed wall, very still.
"Chaitu, you're worried about Dadaji."
He nodded. "Is he going to die?"
Rashmi sat beside him. "Dadaji's heart is tired and weak, and the doctor wants him in the big hospital in town so they can watch him closely. We don't know everything yet. When I know more, I'll tell you. I promise."
Chaitanya thought. "I thought it was worse. Because everyone was whispering."
"No more whispering. You can ask me anything."
"Can I go see him?"
"Sunday. We'll take the bus together."

In their Haifa apartment, Yosef had noticed the boxes in the storeroom and the long phone calls behind closed doors. For a week the ten-year-old had been quiet, eating little.
Daniel finally sat on the edge of his bed. "Yosef, you look worried. Want to tell me?"
"Are you and Ima getting divorced?" Yosef whispered.
Daniel's chest tightened. "No. No, we're not. I'm sorry you've been carrying that." He took a breath. "Here's what's really happening. I got a new job in Toronto. We're moving there in August. The boxes are for that. We didn't tell you because we weren't sure yet, and that was a mistake."
Yosef stared. "Toronto? Is there snow?"
"Lots."
"Will I have friends?"
"Not at first. It'll be hard. We'll help."
Yosef let out a long breath and leaned against his father.

At the parent-teacher meeting in the school hall, Rafiq sat beside his father while Manjula Ma'am opened his report card.
"Maths is improving," she began. "Rafiq worked hard on fractions."
His father sighed. "Improving. His cousin Imran got full marks. Why can't you be more like Imran, Rafiq? Such a genius you are, sixty-two."

Manjula Ma'am put down her pen. "Mr Qureshi, Rafiq started at forty. Sixty-two is a big jump. He stayed back for help three times this month. That tells me a lot about him."
Rafiq looked up, just a little.
On the way out, she stopped him. "Rafiq. You're not Imran. You're you. And you're getting better."

I'm Saurabh, and in Class 10 we had a new physics teacher, Harish Sir, who talked to us like we were in nursery. "Now, children, who can tell me what a magnet does? Very good, beta, clap for him." In front of everyone.
When I asked a real question about why the Earth has a magnetic field, he said, "Such big questions from a small boy! Let's stick to the chapter."

I did. It was the best week of that year.

Dear Didi,

I wanted to tell you about Eshaan's drawing before you saw it and worried.

Yesterday, while you were at work, he showed me a picture: a huge black shape with red eyes behind our building, and a tiny boy running. My first thought was to say, "Eshaan, this is too scary, draw something nice."

I stopped myself and asked, "Tell me about it. What's happening here?"

So we looked out of the window together and watched it come and go. I told him it's just a truck with a very loud engine and a driver who wants to go home.

Today he drew it again, with a smiling driver.

He said, "Masi, next time I'm scared, I'll draw it and tell you."

Love,
Anjali

People ask me what I learnt from a year of babysitting while I studied, and honestly, it's one thing. I'm Ishita, and I learnt it from a six-year-old called Ganga.
One night she wouldn't sleep. She kept pointing at the ceiling fan and crying. My first instinct was the grown-up one: "Ganga, fans don't hurt anyone, close your eyes." I actually had the words ready.
Instead I lay down beside her and asked, "What does the fan do that you don't like?"
She whispered that its shadow, when the fan turned, looked like hands reaching down. And that her brother had said fans can fall.
So we turned on the side lamp so the shadow went away, and I told her the fan was fixed tight, and we tugged on the hook together, standing on the bed.
She slept in ten minutes. A month later, she came to me about the bigger thing, a kid at school being mean. She said, "You always ask first."

qa.q: What did Ganga think the fan's shadow looked like?
qa.a: She said its shadow looked like hands reaching down.

qa.q: Why did Ishita hold back the words she had ready?
qa.a: Ishita sensed Ganga's fear was real and felt curious about what exactly frightened her, instead of impatient to get her to sleep.

qa.q: What would you advise an adult with a scared child at bedtime?
qa.a: Ask what exactly frightens them before reassuring, as Ishita did, then fix what you can, like turning on a lamp.

qa.q: How did Ganga come to see Ishita?
qa.a: Ganga came to trust Ishita as someone who asks first, which is why she later shared a bigger worry about school.

grounding: A young adult asks a child what her fear is about before judging, and the child later brings Ishita a bigger worry.
